# SyberLabs

> SyberLabs builds AI developer tools and interactive web products. Founded by Mateo Robles. Work includes a GitHits design partnership, PorchLight (third place, Cline, Parallel & Composio Hackathon) and RISE.

> **RISE and AI models:** since RISE #294 the RISE server calls no model. An AI reading request runs on the reader’s own connection: hosted Jev through the reader’s OpenRouter account, or a pinned Kev-4B on the reader’s machine (`/kev/` on the site). local Kev did not meet RISE’s bar in internal checks on RISE’s evaluations (RISE `docs/product/tasks/SCR-004.json`), and there is no production Kev deployment, by design. Once the reader connects, RISE’s visual direction sends sections of the reading text to that connection.

This file is generated from the site’s own data (projects/site-data.js in github.com/SyberLabs/SyberLabs.github.io) by scripts/llms.mjs. Each project line carries a "Reflects" stamp: the repository commit and date its claims were checked against. Every project claim is taken from its repository at the commit named in `reflects`, its public page, or docs/SYSTEM_MAPS.md. Evidence states follow MasterMind's discipline: implemented (the behaviour exists in code), tested (a named test exercises it), measured (numbers exist under stated conditions), deployed (it runs somewhere people can reach). Nothing is promoted from one state to the next by wording.

## When to use this file

- Use it to learn what SyberLabs is, which projects exist, what state each one has reached, and where its page, source and live app are.
- Use the "Reflects" commit as the version to read: for code-level questions, read the source repository at that commit (for example with a code index such as GitHits, where the repository is public).
- Quote the evidence lines as written. A project that is implemented or tested is not thereby deployed or measured, and "not yet" lines are part of the claim.
- Read the [full text](https://syberlabs.io/llms-full.txt) for every field each project page shows, including demo captions and run output.

## When not to use this file

- Do not treat it as newer than the Reflects stamp. If a repository has moved on, the repository is the authority for code and this file for what the site claims.
- Do not infer capabilities, users, metrics or deployments that are not stated here; the site states its limits on purpose.
- It describes a website. It is not an API, SDK or package, and it carries no credentials. Never send keys or private data to the contact address.

# Projects

## RISE: Interactive reading app

Page: https://syberlabs.io/projects/rise/
Status: Live · open beta
Reflects: SyberLabs/RISE@998d725 · verified 2026-10-05
Source: https://github.com/SyberLabs/RISE

An interactive reading app that combines text, sound and moving visuals in your browser. Read words at a pace you choose, or switch to a page view.

Page title: RISE: Interactive Reading with Text, Sound and Visuals

Headline: Read beyond the page.

Open beta at rise.syberlabs.io. Reading runs entirely in the browser, and the files and compositions you bring stay in browser storage. An optional AI reading request runs on the reader’s own model connection; once connected, visual direction also sends sections of the reading text there. The RISE server holds no model credential.

Primary link: [Open RISE](https://rise.syberlabs.io/)

Secondary link: [Try the interactive sample](https://rise.syberlabs.io/jev-scene-demo)

Also: [Watch the demo film](https://syberlabs.io/rise-demo/)

Live at [rise.syberlabs.io](https://rise.syberlabs.io/): No account, no key and no install. Pick a reading and press Begin.

### RISE demo film

Video: https://syberlabs.io/rise-demo/rise-marketing-20260929-v3.mp4

Edited from real RISE screen recordings, with an AI-generated narrator and portrait. RISE creates its own abstract visuals and synthesized sound; the film uses an original music bed.

### Why combine reading with sound and visuals?

RISE explores reading as an experience that unfolds over time. Readers can set the pace and combine the words with light and sound, or return to a page view.

The idea is to explore whether the presentation changes how people experience a text. RISE provides browser controls for that exploration. No reader study has established a preference for this approach.

### What you can do today

Five main areas, with related tools grouped inside each one.

- 01 / Home, Begin today’s reading: Home offers one reading with moving visuals behind it. Press Begin, or choose another reading.
- 02 / Read, Stream or Page: Words arrive over time at a pace you set, or sit on a page you can navigate. Switch at any point; your place is kept.
- 03 / Library, Curated public-domain texts: Browse literature, philosophy, poetry and scripture, with records of each edition, its structure and its rights. The Chapel includes the Douay-Rheims Bible and liturgy with timed pacing.
- 04 / Make, Compose your own: Create readings with text, sound and visuals using Workshop, Scriptorium and Visual Lab. Save them in your browser with the Vault.
- 05 / Ask, A reading from your own model: Describe what you want to read. The model chooses a book and presentation only from the supplied catalog. Connect through OpenRouter, or run Kev-4B locally; model requests use your connection and are not billed to SyberLabs.

### Rooms: The five rooms, as they open.

Screenshots of a local build of SyberLabs/RISE@998d725 taken on 2026-10-05 in headless Chromium at 1440×900, nothing mocked. The text in every shot is Rural Architecture, from Lyrical Ballads by Wordsworth and Coleridge, a public-domain work served from RISE’s own Library; the fields behind it are RISE’s procedural engines. A silent 25-second screen recording of the same build, Home → Begin → words arriving in Stream (with the few seconds of Preparing session the software renderer needs), is also available.

Recording: [Watch the screen recording (MP4, 25 s, no sound)](https://syberlabs.io/rise-demo/rooms/rise-rooms-begin-20261005.mp4)

- 01 / Home: Home as it opens: today’s poem, already streaming over its own visual field. (https://syberlabs.io/rise-demo/rooms/rise-home-20261005.webp)
- Menu: The Menu, open on Home: the five rooms, Home, Read, Library, Make and Settings, with Ask for a reading, Guide and Wormhole under More. (https://syberlabs.io/rise-demo/rooms/rise-menu-20261005.webp)
- 02 / Read · Stream: Read, in Stream, ten seconds into a 31-second reading, with the control bar shown: pause, Page view, fullscreen, Visuals, Settings, end. (https://syberlabs.io/rise-demo/rooms/rise-read-stream-20261005.webp)
- 02 / Read · Page: Read, switched to Page view mid-reading: the same poem set as a page under its edition title, the visual field continuing below. (https://syberlabs.io/rise-demo/rooms/rise-read-page-20261005.webp)
- 03 / Library: Library: curated public-domain works in named editions (the Epic shelf opens with Standard Ebooks translations of The Iliad and Metamorphoses), with Chapel, Rosary, Stations, Journeys, Keystones and Provenance as panes. (https://syberlabs.io/rise-demo/rooms/rise-library-20261005.webp)
- 04 / Make: Make, opened from the Menu onto its Workshop pane with Vault, Scriptorium, Visual Lab and Visual Catalog alongside: a new, empty composition; the asset list is the build’s own procedural engines and sourced collections. (https://syberlabs.io/rise-demo/rooms/rise-make-20261005.webp)

### What a model may choose, and what it may not.

How RISE checks an AI reading suggestion, using the rules at 998d725: the model makes one request through your connection and can choose only from the supplied options. Two examples show a suggestion being refused without opening a reading.

Text version of the interactive map: This map needs JavaScript.

### How it is built

- One reading, two views: RISE divides text into timed units, sets the pacing and prepares one reading session. That same session drives both Stream and Page, so switching views keeps your place.
- Book files checked when opened: Book text loads separately from the app, removing 15.4 MB from its JavaScript bundle. Files use SHA-256 content hashes as names, and RISE checks the hash each time it reads a file.
- A limit on initial download size: The initial download is about 59 KB across three requests with Brotli compression. Automated build checks enforce a 64 KB limit.
- No model runs on the RISE server: The Cloudflare Worker serves the app and its catalog of reading choices. It runs no model and holds no model credential. Six retired model-request routes return HTTP 410 (Gone).
- Composer, in ChatGPT: In ChatGPT, RISE lets the model prepare a reading with text, sound and visuals in one tool call. RISE checks the result before making it playable, and the reader presses Begin to start. Rejected readings cannot play.
- Automated checks before release: Around 2,800 Vitest unit and integration tests, plus Playwright browser tests, check the app. Releases also check a generated architecture diagram and the built files, with a way to restore an earlier release.

### Evidence

- deployed: The reader, Library, Chapel, Make rooms and the interactive sample run at rise.syberlabs.io.
- tested: Unit, integration and browser suites run in CI; the first-load budget and the design diagram are checked on every release.
- measured: Composer in ChatGPT: a controlled developer-mode session on 2026-10-04 produced an admitted Current and narration the reader confirmed hearing. That is partial acceptance on one release, not a public listing.
- tested: RISE Plus voice, an optional ElevenLabs voice ($8.99 a month): implementation merged; paid launch pending verification. It runs in production on Stripe test mode: on 2026-10-08 a test purchase unlocked it and the voice was heard reading the buyer's own file.
- not yet: No reader study has been run; release evidence still records zero real-device and stranger-testing records.

### Facts

- Runs in: Any modern browser at rise.syberlabs.io
- Technology: JavaScript (ES modules), Vite, Web Audio API, Canvas 2D, IndexedDB, Cloudflare Workers, Vitest, Playwright, GitHub Actions
- AI integration: Optional and reader-owned: Connect OpenRouter (TypeSafe AI’s hosted Jev), or run RISE locally with a pinned Kev-4B; there is no production Kev deployment, by design.
- Privacy: Texts you bring and compositions you make stay in your browser. Once you connect your own AI, visual direction sends sections of the reading text to that connection (a text you bring, only with your consent). See the app’s posted Privacy and Terms.
- License: Apache 2.0 for application code; texts and visual works carry their own terms
- Composer in Claude: Live as a custom connector: add one named RISE with the URL https://rise.syberlabs.io/api/mcp. Submission to Claude’s connector directory is planned.
- Earlier evidence: [Jev integration in RISE](https://syberlabs.io/jev/)
- Your own model: [Reader-owned AI: Jev and Kev](https://syberlabs.io/kev/)
- RISE Plus: [Optional voice, your own reading read aloud: paid launch pending verification](https://syberlabs.io/plus/)
- Source: [github.com/SyberLabs/RISE](https://github.com/SyberLabs/RISE)

## FLYSPACE: Visual data workspace

Page: https://syberlabs.io/projects/flyspace/
Status: Live preview
Reflects: SyberLabs/Flyspace@e95ae73 · verified 2026-10-05
Source: https://github.com/SyberLabs/Flyspace

A visual workspace where you connect data sources to AI assistants and see which sources feed each answer. AI answers require running FLYSPACE locally with your own model, for example through Ollama. Formerly OmniOS.

Page title: FLYSPACE: Connect Data Sources to AI Assistants

Headline: See the sources behind an answer.

A limited public preview is live at omni.syberlabs.io: the canvas, the Shell Store and every keyless public data source run in your browser. AI answers and keyed sources are switched off there.

Primary link: [Open the preview](https://omni.syberlabs.io/)

Secondary link: [Run it locally](https://github.com/SyberLabs/Flyspace#run)

Also: [View source](https://github.com/SyberLabs/Flyspace)

Live at [omni.syberlabs.io](https://omni.syberlabs.io/): The preview opens as OmniOS. Your canvas stays in your browser.

### The morning: one question, cited sources, a crystal, a second persona

Video: https://syberlabs.io/omni-demo/omnios-morning-20261005.mp4

Recorded on 2026-10-05 from a local production build of OmniOS@e95ae73, following the “morning” journey specified by its acceptance test. The blocks and two AI answers use fixed test data, not live markets or a live model. The canvas, connections, source labels and answer history are the real interface. Silent, 30 seconds.

### Why a canvas.

FLYSPACE shows which data an AI assistant receives. A canvas displays the sources, their connections and whether they supplied any data.

Each answer records the source data used to produce it, including data passed through other AI assistants. Sources that supplied no data are not cited.

### What you can do in the preview

The first three steps work in the public preview. AI questions and voice controls require a local setup with a model connection.

- 01 / Shell, Open a saved workspace: The Shell Store opens saved workspaces. The Investor workspace connects Polymarket, CoinGecko, World Bank and Hacker News to an Analyst assistant, then connects that assistant to a Strategist.
- 02 / Blocks, Pull real numbers: Add blocks for prediction markets, crypto prices, economic series, research and news. Every built-in source is public and needs no key.
- 03 / Wires, Say what feeds what: Connect a data block to an AI assistant. FLYSPACE checks that their input and output formats match. If they do not, it explains the mismatch and leaves the workspace unchanged.
- 04 / Ask, Ask with your own model: Ask an assistant a question. Its answer cites only the sources connected to it. A record identifies the model provider, model, response time and source data used.
- 05 / Talk, Spoken canvas control: Hold Talk and use a supported command such as “wire hacker news to the analyst”, “delete this” or “undo”. The app checks the request, previews deletion and asks for clearer names when a request is ambiguous.

### Which sources reach an answer.

The Investor shell, stepped through by rule: a feed fails, a feed goes stale, and the record says exactly which sources each answer used. Open any node to see who owns it.

Text version of the interactive map: This map needs JavaScript.

### How it is built

- Sources, connections and assistants: A block shows one data source. A wire connects it only after the app checks that connection. An AI assistant, called a persona in the app, answers using its active incoming connections and cannot select its own inputs.
- Check data formats before connecting: The app checks declared input and output formats when you create a connection. A mismatch is refused unless you choose a text-only conversion. Blocks without declared formats can still connect without that check.
- Record how each answer was made: An optional PostgreSQL database records each model request and the exact source data used. It also records answers passed between assistants, so you can trace them after source data changes. The canvas stays in browser storage (IndexedDB) and works without a server.
- Review tools before allowing changes: Tool descriptions become a list of available actions, called a capability manifest. It can be built from OpenAPI documents, MCP tool schemas or a structured description and registered with one function. Actions that write or delete data require approval; the list cannot grant itself permission. Unique request keys prevent duplicates, and uncertain results remain marked uncertain.
- Keys stay server-side: Model-provider keys are read from the server environment and never sent to the browser. Automated builds substitute detectable test values for secrets and fail if any value appears in browser code.
- Limits of the public preview: The public preview disables paid model requests, sources requiring keys and access to the model-request history at the server routes. The setup checklist is published with the code.

### Evidence

- deployed: The limited public preview has run at omni.syberlabs.io since 2026-10-03, deployed by hand from a recorded commit on Cloudflare Workers.
- tested: Unit tests across the stores, services and capability engine, and six Playwright specs including the “morning” golden path: shell → question → cited sources → crystal → second persona.
- implemented: The capability compiler and the server-side broker are implemented and hardened against fixtures and stubbed transports.
- not yet: No third-party API or MCP server has been measured in production use. Speech is tested with typed transcripts; there is no live microphone measurement. The hosted identity boundary exists in code with no provisioned issuer.

### Facts

- Stage: Local-first, single-user app with a limited public preview
- Formerly: OmniOS, renamed in October 2026; the preview address, omni.syberlabs.io, keeps the old name for now
- Technology: TypeScript, Next.js, React, Zustand, IndexedDB, PostgreSQL (optional), Tailwind CSS, Vitest, Playwright, Cloudflare Workers
- AI models: Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, and local models through Ollama; optional Kev persona suggestions
- Data sources: Polymarket, CoinGecko, Hacker News, World Bank, OpenAlex, Metaculus, NewsAPI (keyed)
- License: No license file yet; the repository is public
- Source: [github.com/SyberLabs/Flyspace](https://github.com/SyberLabs/Flyspace)

## SyberWork: AI work review tools

Page: https://syberlabs.io/projects/syberwork/
Status: Work in progress
Reflects: SyberLabs/SyberWork@208eaf6 · verified 2026-10-05
Source: https://github.com/SyberLabs/SyberWork

Tools for checking and approving AI work before it makes changes. Rules define the allowed steps, a named person approves the work, and a tamper-evident history records what was proposed, checked, approved and done.

Page title: SyberWork: Review and Approval Tools for AI Work

Headline: Check AI work before it changes anything.

Build Thread applies these checks to code changes in your Git repository. It runs the checks itself before accepting a change, even if the model says the tests passed. Actions use unique keys to prevent duplicate execution, and their results are checked afterwards.

Primary link: [View source](https://github.com/SyberLabs/SyberWork)

Secondary link: [Build Thread in ten minutes](https://github.com/SyberLabs/SyberWork/blob/main/docs/BUILD_THREAD.md)

### Why check each proposed step?

When an AI proposes an action, people need to know who approved it, what evidence supported it and whether it succeeded. SyberWork checks each proposal against rules controlled by the system running it.

The rules define what may happen and who can approve it. If a proposal breaks a rule, SyberWork refuses it and records the reason and the rule used. The same checks can apply to a purchase order or a code change.

### Build Thread: review one code change

Python 3.11+ and git. No account, no model and no network required.

- 01 / init, Name your real checks: syberlabs init writes a contract into .syberlabs/ and guesses the test command. When it cannot, it writes a check that fails until you name one, so an unchecked change never looks accepted.
- 02 / start, Open a thread: A thread tracks one change to one repository and names the files it may affect. It records and checks the starting Git commit.
- 03 / propose, Keep proposed edits separate: Your edit, a coding tool’s edit, or an automated search result is saved as a separate Git commit for review. It does not change your working files.
- 04 / check, The host runs the checks: Checks run against the exact proposed files. The record keeps their exit codes, how long they took and hashes of their output.
- 05 / accept and publish, Accept the change, then choose what to publish: Accept updates one branch only if it still points to the expected commit. Pushing code, opening a pull request and publishing each require a separate allowed action, with duplicate prevention and recovery checks.

### A model’s claim is not a result.

The repository’s own Build Thread example, run on 2026-10-05 from SyberWork@208eaf6 with Python 3.11 and git. No model, no network.

```
$ PYTHONPATH=. python examples/build_thread.py
{
  "context": ["tests/test_report.py:1-7", "src/report.py:1-2"],
  "model": {
    "candidate": "c1",
    "claimed": { "tests": "passed", "confidence": 0.97 },
    "verdict": "candidate_check_failed:tests",
    "accept": "denied:candidate_check_failed:tests"
  },
  "patch": {
    "candidate": "c2",
    "verdict": "all_checks_passed",
    "accept": "succeeded",
    "branch": "refs/heads/syberlabs/e643ed26",
    "commit": "7c606ae8f44f3f999c010799e1d2fdcee1166011"
  },
  "working_tree_and_main_untouched": true,
  "resumed": { "status": "complete", "accepted": "c2", "events": 18, "chain_valid": true },
  "replay_under_v2": ["candidate_check_missing:lint", "candidate_check_missing:lint"]
}
build-thread complete
```

The provider claimed c1 passed its tests with 0.97 confidence, but checks run on its exact files failed, so SyberWork rejected it. Candidate c2 passed all checks. It was accepted by updating one branch only after confirming the branch had not changed (compare-and-swap). The working files and main branch were untouched. The thread resumed from a valid 18-event history. Replaying that history with a new lint-check requirement shows both candidates would be rejected for the missing check.

### How it is built

- Separate the core from the app: The reusable syberlabs package defines the rules, proposal interface and in-memory Session. It uses a fixed JSON format and a hash-linked event history. The syberwork app adds storage, a web API, command-line tools, a console and connectors. The core never imports the app.
- A chain you can verify: Every case event is hashed into a chain with a canonical-JSON digest and rule id beside it, an HMAC witness, an Ed25519 signature of the chain head, and an append-only transparency log kept in a separate file by a witness process that holds the key.
- A fixed format for exchanging work records: Fifteen JSON schemas define work rules, observations, proposals, approval decisions, actions, outcome checks and rule changes. The protocol is sdk.syberlabs.space/v0alpha1, with a format checker and reference event sequences.
- Plan checks and review rule changes: The compiler turns the work rules into ordered steps, approval checks, completion checks and form fields. Replay shows how changed rules would apply to recorded history without calling a model, changing a destination or fetching live data.
- Separate proposals from execution: A planner receives the objective, allowed actions, work rules, history and completion criteria, then proposes one action. It cannot execute the action. It can run through an HTTPS service or a local loopback address.
- Prevent duplicate writes: Executors send writes with unique request keys and conditions that prevent duplicates or outdated changes, then record the receipt. If the outcome is uncertain, it stays marked uncertain rather than being retried blindly.

### Evidence

- tested: Twenty-three golden conformance traces, a clean-install release gate and CI green on CPython 3.11 to 3.13.
- measured: On the author’s machine with the default SQLite sync: explain.allowed median 3.8 µs, complete_case median 37.4 ms, chain verification of 501 events median 10.2 ms.
- implemented: The included procurement case runs end to end against a separate reference system, with a real order POST under an idempotency key and manager sign-off.
- not yet: The service binds to loopback and has no deployment beyond one machine. No outside project consumes the SDK. The model-versus-patch benchmark has not been run against a real model.

### Facts

- Stage: Open-source runtime and SDK, version 0.1.0, wheel verified
- Technology: Python 3.11+ with no runtime dependencies, SQLite, pytest; Docker files for the console
- License: Apache 2.0
- Source: [github.com/SyberLabs/SyberWork](https://github.com/SyberLabs/SyberWork)

## Relay: Job application workspace

Page: https://syberlabs.io/projects/relay/
Status: Early release
Reflects: SyberLabs/relay@0000605 · verified 2026-10-05
Source: https://github.com/SyberLabs/relay

A workspace for job seekers who draft with AI assistants, with one record per job and human approval of the exact wording.

Page title: Relay: Job Application Workspace for AI-Assisted Drafting

Headline: Every application has a history.

Relay works alongside ChatGPT, Codex, Claude, Grok and your notes in Notion or Obsidian. Each job keeps its research, confirmed facts and draft versions in one history. Relay never submits an employer form.

Primary link: [View source](https://github.com/SyberLabs/relay)

Secondary link: [Integration setup](https://github.com/SyberLabs/relay/blob/main/integrations/README.md)

### Why keep one history per application?

People already hunt for jobs with ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Notion and Obsidian. The work falls apart in the gaps: a new chat forgets the last draft, a tracker overwrites a decision, an interview note resets an application’s status.

Relay keeps research and draft history for each job. Approval applies to one exact draft. Returned work must match the job and its current version, so an old draft cannot silently replace newer reviewed work.

### How a job moves through Relay

Fictional example records ship with the app.

- 01 / Import, Bring the research: Add a job from a title and posting URL, pull a public Greenhouse or Lever board, map a tracker CSV, or import notes from Notion or Obsidian. Matching URLs join the same record.
- 02 / Facts, Confirm what is true: Confirm facts about your experience in a reusable list. Relay checks selected claim patterns in AI drafts against those facts and flags unsupported claims. These checks do not verify whether a fact is true.
- 03 / Draft, Hand off to your assistant: Export the job’s research and drafting instructions for ChatGPT, Codex or Claude, then import the draft for the same job version. Browsers supporting WebMCP, a tool connection for browser assistants, can let an assistant place a draft directly in the review queue.
- 04 / Accept, Approve the exact words: Acceptance records approval of one draft version. Change the text and it needs review again.
- 05 / Send and record, You press submit: After a person uses Inspect Accept to approve the form details, Relay’s Chrome extension can fill the form once. You still press submit. The outcome is recorded with a receipt.

### Screens: Four screens from a local build.

Captured on 2026-10-05 from relay@0000605 built and run locally with its own migrations and the mocked local sign-in. Every company, role and fact shown is a fictional example record; no real applicant data.

- Runtime with a fictional example job selected. Approve & send stays disabled until an agent prepares the application. (https://syberlabs.io/relay-demo/relay-runtime-20261005.jpg)
- Review and approve one exact draft. Nothing is sent. (https://syberlabs.io/relay-demo/relay-accept-20261005.jpg)
- Tracker. Three fictional jobs by status; imported submissions without a receipt stay visible but are excluded from reply rates. (https://syberlabs.io/relay-demo/relay-tracker-20261005.jpg)
- The fact ledger. Two fictional facts confirmed by the user and available for agent citations; Relay records the confirmation and does not verify facts itself. (https://syberlabs.io/relay-demo/relay-facts-20261005.jpg)

### What leaves Relay, and what comes back.

Recorded by running the repository’s own modules: research sent to an assistant, the returned draft, checks of the job identity, version and claims, and five rejected examples that write nothing.

Text version of the interactive map: This map needs JavaScript.

### How it is built

- One history per job: Posting observations are preserved as rows; rediscovery keeps an existing interview or submitted status instead of resetting it.
- Reject outdated drafts: Research sent to an assistant and drafts returned for review carry the job identity and version. Relay rejects work based on an outdated version.
- Claim checks: Relay compares words and numbers in a draft with the confirmed facts it cites. This is an approximate check and is labelled as such; it does not establish factual truth.
- Edge deployment: TypeScript and React on Cloudflare Workers with Drizzle ORM, a Manifest V3 extension, and Playwright tests.

### Evidence

- tested: The domain, handoff and profile modules were executed under Node for the site’s recorded Relay map; the D1 acceptance write is reproduced as a rule.
- implemented: Runtime, Tracker, the fact ledger, CSV and job-board import, and every integration listed in the repository.
- not yet: No public deployment and no customer counts, hiring outcomes or throughput improvements are claimed. Autonomous hunting is not included.

### Facts

- Built by: Seth Carlson and Mateo Robles
- Technology: TypeScript, React, Vinext, Cloudflare Workers, D1, Drizzle ORM, Chrome extension (Manifest V3), Playwright
- Boundary: Relay prepares and tracks application materials. It does not submit employer forms, host an MCP connection, or sync accounts in the background.
- Source: [github.com/SyberLabs/relay](https://github.com/SyberLabs/relay)

## OSAHR: Network simulation library

Page: https://syberlabs.io/projects/osahr/
Status: Research
Reflects: SyberLabs/OSAHR_Cell@7293e27 · verified 2026-10-05
Source: https://github.com/SyberLabs/OSAHR_Cell

An open-source Python library for simulating networks whose connections change over time. Rules and probabilities determine each change, and recorded runs can be replayed and checked.

Page title: OSAHR: Simulate Changing Networks in Python

Headline: Replay a changing system.

The simulator represents connections that can join several items at once, then changes them at random times using exact probabilities. Every public claim is graded Known, Measured, Inferred or Proposed.

Primary link: [View source](https://github.com/SyberLabs/OSAHR_Cell)

Secondary link: [Read the architecture](https://github.com/SyberLabs/OSAHR_Cell/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md)

### Why simulate changing connections?

Most simulators change the state of a fixed network. Many real systems change the network itself: a cell grows a connection, an organisation adds a role, an agent fleet forms a new channel. Modelling that exactly, with the right probabilities and a record you can replay, is the problem OSAHR takes on.

The simulation core is small and has no external dependencies, making its rules easier to state and check. It is intended as a foundation for the lab’s work approval tools.

### What you can do

Install the Python package with pip, or download the source and run its examples.

- 01 / Model, Define the network and its rules: Define the kinds of items and connections in the network, the patterns each rule can change, and how often those changes can occur. Rules can also update settings and memory.
- 02 / Run, Choose a scheduler: Choose how the simulator schedules changes: Direct SSA, modified next-reaction or bounded thinning. All three preserve the exact probabilities. The faster pattern search is checked against a search of every possibility.
- 03 / Replay, Reproduce every state: Use the same random seed to repeat a run. Replay can also apply each recorded change and verify the hash, a fingerprint of the simulation state, at every step.
- 04 / Review, Review recorded experiments: The decision workbench packages recorded experiments for review with labels for their evidence level. GrokCell is a prototype for coordinating AI agents on the same simulation core.

### Watch network connections change one event at a time.

Recorded by running the adaptive-signal example and exported from the trace.

Text version of the interactive map: This map needs JavaScript.

### Twenty-five events, one hash to replay.

The repository’s own example, run on 2026-10-05 from OSAHR_Cell@7293e27 with Python 3.11 in a fresh venv after python -m pip install -e . No dependencies, no network.

```
$ python examples/adaptive_signal.py
events: 25
simulation time: 10.000000
agents: 2
receiver: {'active': True, 'value': 2.5, 'responsiveness': 1.0}
memory: {'received_count': 10, 'intensity_ema': 0.17478781247500003}
state hash: 6d73af0a24684c9afc339e1bc59dddbd6ca42a08792fca5b8b7e123fc262a857
```

Complete output, unedited. With random seed 20260729, the simulation recorded 25 events in ten units of simulated time. Two agents exchanged ten received signals. The receiver’s value rose to 2.5 and its responsiveness rose from 0.1 to the limit of 1.0, through an external event at t = 3 and changes made by the rule itself. The state hash fingerprints the final state. A second run with the same seed prints the same lines.

### How it is built

- Changes with exact probabilities: Rules change network connections at random times while preserving their exact probabilities. The network is a typed directed hypergraph, whose connections can link several items at once. Its required properties are documented in the architecture guide.
- Recheck only affected patterns: After a change, the simulator searches affected connections for rule matches. This incremental search is checked against a search of every possible match.
- Adaptive parameters: Rules can update the model’s settings and memory, changing how it behaves as its connections change.
- No runtime dependencies: The core runs on Python 3.11+ without extra packages. Recorded experiments document checks of that core.

### Evidence

- tested: A pytest suite of 41 test files across the kernel, experiments and workbench; the kernel suite (tests/) passed 127 of 128 on 2026-10-05, the one skip being the optional ontology probe. Replay of the site’s recorded trace reproduces every state hash.
- implemented: Kernel, three schedulers, incremental matching, adaptive parameters, replay, the decision workbench and the GrokCell prototype.
- not yet: Research models of mechanisms, not calibrated forecasts. No continuous integration is configured in the repository yet.

### Facts

- Stage: Open-source research library, version 0.2.1
- Technology: Python 3.11+ (no runtime dependencies in the core library), pytest
- License: Apache 2.0 in the LICENSE file; pyproject.toml’s metadata still says MIT
- Source: [github.com/SyberLabs/OSAHR_Cell](https://github.com/SyberLabs/OSAHR_Cell)
